summary:
Atul Ramachandran, CTO and co-founder of Filed Inc, presents a framework for building vertical AI products that move beyond chat and citations. He argues that vertical SaaS products typically promise time and cost savings but fail because chat is synchronous—users must wait for responses—and citations merely shift the verification burden back to the customer, adding extra work rather than removing it. This is especially problematic in verticals like healthcare, legal, and taxes where every error feels catastrophic.

He traces product evolution through three abstraction levels using a bank metaphor: physical presence (bottleneck = employee count), digital transformation (bottleneck = user count), and agentic delegation (user-visit bottleneck removed entirely). In the agentic era, users come to delegate work, not to operate the product themselves, meaning value generation is no longer capped by user visit frequency.

He introduces a conveyor belt model where AI agents are workers and users are supervisors. To build this, he identifies four key components. First, delegation: find tasks taking more than a couple of hours that are repeatable, and build long-running background agents. Second, skills: capture the last 20% of work—the quirks, preferences, and conventions specific to each user or firm—automatically from product usage rather than requiring a separate interface. Third, monitoring: provide task lists and traces so users can see what agents did and how. Fourth, control: ensure users can pause, intervene, and resume—taking the wheel rather than abandoning the car.

He adds that physical bank branches did not disappear with mobile banking, and similarly all layers coexist. Users will only delegate work if they trust they can take back control, so products must retain level two (digital) features alongside agentic features to build trust. For irreversible or dangerous actions, products must present a plan for approval before execution—like Filed showing a plan before data entry that could overwrite existing tax data.

Finally, he argues that weekly active users is the wrong metric for agentic products. Instead, products should measure weekly active sessions—tasks completed by humans or agents even when users are absent. The goal is for weekly active users to decline while weekly active sessions increase, reflecting successful delegation. His three key takeaways: design for delegation not participation, think of products as conveyor belts where users supervise, and change measurement from time on platform to weekly active sessions.

sections.title: Introduction: Chat and Citations Won't Save Vertical AI
sections.summary: Atul introduces the thesis: vertical AI products promise time and cost savings, but the primary interfaces—chat for input and citations for output—cannot keep this promise.

sections.title: Speaker Background and Filed Inc
sections.summary: Atul introduces himself as CTO and co-founder of Filed, which builds products for US tax professionals. Filed has raised over $17M and has seen tremendous growth.

sections.title: Benefits and Limitations of Chat and Citations
sections.summary: Chat enables flexible interaction and fast building; citations ground answers in truth and reduce hallucinations. But chat is synchronous and citations put the verification burden back on the customer, adding extra work in vertical industries where accuracy is critical.

sections.title: Three Levels of Product Abstraction: The Bank Metaphor
sections.summary: Products have evolved through three abstraction levels. Physical presence: users delegate to employees (bottleneck = employee count). Digital transformation: users self-serve via apps (bottleneck = user count). Agentic delegation: users delegate work to AI agents (user-visit bottleneck removed).

sections.title: The Conveyor Belt Model and Designing for Delegation
sections.summary: Agentic products are like a conveyor belt: AI agents are workers, users are supervisors who delegate and monitor. The core principle is to design for delegation, not participation. Four key components are needed: delegation, skills, monitoring, and control.

sections.title: Component 1: Delegation of Long-Running Tasks
sections.summary: Find tasks that take more than a couple of hours and are repeatable. In taxes, Filed identified three such tasks. These become long-running background agents that remove hours of work.

sections.title: Component 2: Skills Capture the Last 20%
sections.summary: Every user has preferences and conventions. Background agents get 80-90% done, but the last 20% requires capturing skills—quirks of how users do the work. Filed captures these automatically from product usage.

sections.title: Components 3 and 4: Monitoring and Control
sections.summary: Monitoring requires task lists and traces showing how agents produced each value, building trust and visibility. Control means users can pause, fix problems, and resume—taking the wheel, not abandoning the car. Users can tag agents and respond to conflicts.

sections.title: Trust, Irreversible Actions, and Plan Approval
sections.summary: Physical bank branches didn't disappear with mobile banking; similarly, all abstraction layers coexist. Users will only delegate work if they trust they can take back control, so products must retain digital-era features. For irreversible or dangerous actions, products must present a plan for approval before execution—like Filed showing a plan before data entry that could overwrite existing tax data.

sections.title: Changing Metrics: Weekly Active Sessions
sections.summary: Since agentic products are built for delegation, not participation, weekly active users is the wrong metric. The appropriate measure is weekly active sessions—tasks completed by humans or agents even when users are absent. The aim is for weekly active users to decline while weekly active sessions increase, reflecting successful delegation.

sections.title: Key Takeaways and Conclusion
sections.summary: Three key takeaways: design for delegation not participation, think of products as conveyor belts where users are supervisors, and change measurement from time on platform to weekly active sessions. Atul closes by wishing the audience luck.
